articles.title: Sonay Kartal misses out on maiden WTA 1000 title in Wuhan Open final defeat to Maja Chwalinska
articles.summary: Britain's Sonay Kartal missed out on a maiden WTA 1000 title after losing to Maja Chwalinska in the Wuhan Open final; Kartal had won the opening set but French Open runner-up Chwalinska brilliantly fought back to win in three sets
articles.body:
Kartal led by a set and a break as she looked to become just the second Briton, after Johanna Konta, to win a WTA 1000 title but French Open finalist Chwalinska produced a superb display to fight back and win 2-6 6-4 6-2.

Nevertheless, it has still been a remarkable week for Kartal, the best in her career so far, after only returning to the tour earlier this month following a six-month lay-off due to a back injury.

"That was one heck of a battle, Maja," said Kartal, who will become the new British No 1 on Monday.

"I hope I can be in many more of these finals. It was not the result I wanted today but those people in my box are the reason I am healthy, I am here and why I am back to fitness."

Kartal was 170th in the WTA rankings prior to the Wuhan Open but her run to the final will see her return to the top 50 after impressive wins over Belinda Bencic, Jasmine Paolini, Elina Svitolina and Jelena Ostapenko.

It is arguably the most impressive tournament performance from a British female player since Emma Raducanu won the 2021 US Open.

"We have had an unbelievable week. Not many people expected me to be here and bring these levels, so thank you, guys," said Kartal.

How Chwalinska denied Kartal in topsy-turvy Wuhan Open final

In Sunday's final, Kartal came flying out of the blocks, showcasing the excellent variety she has displayed all week in Wuhan to break early and race into a 2-0 lead in the opening set.

Chwalinska broke back before Kartal restored her break advantage and led 4-1 before going on to claim the first set in 45 minutes by simply overpowering the Pole.

The dream week looked to be becoming a reality when Kartal broke early in the second set, only for Chwalinska to find a way to counter her opponent's canny game by suddenly raising her aggression levels.

Chwalinska got back on level terms and forced Kartal to work hard to hold, with the Briton having faced more than 50 points on serve compared to Chwalinska's 15 at one point in the middle of the set.

The turning point came when Chwalinska went 4-3 up to break in the second set. Even though Kartal broke straight back to make it 4-4, the momentum had completely changed as Chwalinska broke again then held serve to take the final into a deciding set.

The opening four games were shared, but perhaps the effects of returning to competitive action only last month began to catch up with Kartal as fatigue set in.

Chwalinska started to come out on top in the longer rallies she had been losing earlier in the match, reeling off four consecutive games to claim the biggest title of her career.

Davidovich Fokina battles back to beat Jodar in Shanghai

It was a similar story at the Shanghai Masters final as Spain's Alejandro Davidovich Fokina won his first ATP 1000 title after beating compatriot Rafael Jodar 1-6 7-6 (7-5) 6-4.

Davidovich Fokina was a set and a break down but fought back, saving more break points in a close second set, before digging deep to defeat up and coming star Jodar.

"I don't have any words right now. I have a blank mind. I don't know what to say and I don't know how I feel. Just a huge relief," said Davidovich Fokina, who will rise to 13th in the ATP rankings.

"After the first set I had to keep trying, keep pushing, like every match in the tournament. In the tie-break, I believed in myself again and tried to play the ball. He was playing huge tennis.

"In the third set, maybe I had a bit more fitness physically. He's an amazing player and it was very tough to play against him today."

articles.title: Mirra Andreeva and Erika Andreeva: Family sacrifices, their journey from Siberia to professional tennis, and the sacrifices that shaped their rise on the international circuit
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable story of Mirra and Erika Andreeva, two sisters from Siberia who conquered the challenges of professional tennis with family support and dedication. Explore their rise to fame, sacrifices made, and the dynamics of sibling rivalry in the competitive world of sports.
articles.body: Mirra Andreeva and Erika Andreeva started their professional tennis careers in Krasnoyarsk, Siberia, where the winters are so cold that it is hard to play outside all year. Their family’s persistence in giving the sisters better opportunities has led to major relocations, new coaching environments and years of dedication to the sport.Erika, born in 2004, started her career on the junior circuit before Mirra, born in 2007, followed a similar path. Three years older, Erika had been through the rigors of competitive tennis first and set an example for her younger sister of what life as a pro entailed.How Mirra Andreeva and Erika Andreeva rose from Siberia to tennis prominenceBoth sisters made the mark as promising juniors. Erika was a finalist in the girls’ singles at the 2021 French Open and Mirra was a runner-up in the girls’ singles at the 2023 Australian Open. While their accomplishments showed the family’s growing presence in the international game, their professional careers eventually diverged in pace.Mirra had a breakthrough in 2023, when she began to turn heads internationally with solid showings at big events. In 2024, she reached the semifinals of the French Open and won her first WTA singles title later that year. In 2025, she won the Dubai and Indian Wells WTA 1000 titles, becoming the youngest champion at this level of tournament since it was introduced in 2009.In June 2026, Mirra took another step, winning her first Grand Slam singles title at the French Open, beating Poland’s Maja Chwalinska in the final. The win was a major milestone for the younger sister, who had been buoyed by the experience and example of her older sister.Raisa Andreeva’s vision and family sacrifices behind their tennis careersThe sisters' journey was largely shaped by their mother Raisa Andreeva, who introduced them to tennis and nurtured their development from a young age, and speaking about how her mother picked the sport for the family, Mirra said she was happy with the decision as tennis felt like a natural fit for her.Evidently, Raisa had gotten interested in the game before Erika was born. Watching tennis was an inspiration to her, including Russian player Marat Safin’s victory in the 2005 Australian Open, and she nurtured the ambition of seeing her daughters play the sport professionally. But to make that dream a reality required more than just regular classes; it meant moving to places with better training opportunities.The first big move was from Krasnoyarsk to Sochi, where the climate was milder and offered better opportunities for tennis practice, and in 2022, the sisters took their next big step and moved to Cannes, France, to train at the Elite Tennis Center with coaches Jean-René Lisnard and Jean-Christophe Faurel.Moving to France brought the sisters closer to the international tennis scene, but it also meant the family had to adjust to life in another country as they supported two developing professional athletes. Training, travel, accommodation and tournament participation all took time, money and careful planning before the sisters could take their place on the professional circuit.Their mother did more than just bring them to the sport. She attended tournaments and remained engaged, which helped maintain the family connection in the face of the pressures of pro competition, and their story reflects how the rise of an athlete has often been dependent on a larger support system, particularly in the early years when results and earnings are uncertain.The sisters learned from each other, too. Mirra has said Erika helped her understand what it takes to compete, including playing tournaments, and how to juggle schoolwork and tennis. In 2026, Mirra told her older sister she was a role model, knowing she had benefited from taking a path that Erika had already started.Mirra Andreeva and Erika Andreeva navigate rivalry and sisterhoodThe sisters share a sporting background, but their professional careers have taken different directions. Mirra is one of the top players of her generation, while Erika has had periods of inconsistent results and a difficult spell away from the competition.Erika achieved a career-high singles ranking of No. 65 in October 2024. But she took time off the circuit for a few months before coming back after failing to find her form and mental health in 2025. Her return has been about building up her confidence and gradually working her way back through the lower-tier events.Mirra’s ascent has had its own challenges, most notably when the sisters have met in professional matches. The pair first met at the Wuhan Open in October 2024, where Erika prevailed in straight sets. The pair met again at the Stuttgart Open in April 2025, but Erika retired with an injury to her right knee when trailing Mirra 6-2, 1-0.Mirra says playing against her sister is emotionally different than playing against anyone else. She has said her focus can be drawn to how Erika is doing instead of being completely on her own performance. Even at the professional level of tennis, the closeness of the relationship makes the experience particularly complicated.The sisters have also made efforts to keep their relationship from getting too competitive. They have been encouraged by their parents to focus on their bond, and have not been regularly playing competitive points against each other in practice. It allows them to teach and help each other without every interaction being a competition.Erika has also said she is proud of Mirra’s accomplishments, even as she works to rebuild her own career. Their experiences show that just because they play the same sport doesn’t mean the same outcome. Their relationship is more a case of mutual understanding, individual ambition and the challenges of the competing demands of careers within the same family.The Andreeva sisters' saga isn't just about rankings and trophies; it's a story that goes from Siberia to the international tennis circuit, and it speaks to the moves, family commitment and personal adjustments that accompany professional sport, and the importance of keeping a close sibling relationship while following individual goals.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 7 Players Withdraw from WTA Ningbo and Osaka
articles.summary: The tennis season is finally winding down, but there is still no shortage of tournaments to follow in the last few weeks. On the women’s side, a WTA 500 in N...
articles.body:
The tennis season is finally winding down, but there is still no shortage of tournaments to follow in the last few weeks. On the women's side, a WTA 500 in Ningbo and a WTA 250 in Osaka will kickstart the final stretch. Several players are ending their seasons early, taking time off, or preparing for the WTA finals.

7 Players Withdraw from WTA Ningbo and Osaka

Which Players Have Withdrawn from Ningbo?

It's been a strange post- US Open swing for Jessica Pegula as she withdrew from Beijing and lost in her opening match of Wuhan to Jelena Ostapenko in three sets. That isn't necessarily a bad loss, as Ostapenko showcased her good form in a semifinal run, but certainly not up to the standards Pegula has set for herself this year. With her WTA Finals spot secure, she's withdrawn from Ningbo, giving herself time to prepare for the last tournament of the year.

Elina Svitolina has also secured her appearance at the WTA Finals and has withdrawn from Ningbo as well. Svitolina lost in the quarterfinals of Wuhan to Sonay Kartal, a loss that, like Pegula's, was later proven to be against a quality opponent. Svitolina is still on the entry list for Tokyo, but she's able to take this week off due to securing her spot at the year-end championships.

The final withdrawal from Ningbo is Anna Kalinskaya, who retired in her opening match in Beijing and withdrew from Wuhan due to injury.

Who Replaced Those Players in the Main Draw?

Leylah Fernandez, who tends to find success in this part of the season, entered the main draw as a result of Pegula's withdrawal. Fernandez's status as an alternate shows how strong the draw is, as Fernandez currently sits at No. 30 in the live WTA rankings. Fernandez is also the defending champion in Osaka, but she opted to go to Ningbo this year instead, with the opportunity to defend her points and pick up even more.

Taking Kalinskaya's place in the main draw is Diane Parry, a player on a four-match losing streak starting from the US Open. Parry had a good run of form up to that point, though, and like Fernandez she isn't far from the top 30.

Svitolina's late withdrawal made room for a lucky loser, a spot taken by Anhelina Kalinina. Kalinina gave a walkover in her second-round qualifying match but was still able to enter the main draw.

Which Players Have Withdrawn from Osaka?

Following her monumental title run in Beijing, Qinwen Zheng won't be playing in Osaka. She withdrew from Wuhan as well, able to be more selective with her schedule now that she's back in the upper echelon of the rankings. Also taking a break after an excellent run is Nikola Bartunkova, who made the Beijing semifinals before losing early in Wuhan.

Both Camila Osorio and Clara Tauson gave walkovers in their first-round matches in Wuhan, and as such they won't be participating in the action in Osaka.

Playing for the first time since her maiden WTA title a few weeks ago, Kaitlin Quevedo was able to enter the main draw due to Osorio's withdrawal. Despite that title run, Quevedo has yet to break the top 70 but has shown her potential over the course of this year.

Osaka doubles pairing Caty McNally and Ashlyn Krueger both entered the main draw as alternates, with McNally replacing Tauson and Krueger replacing Zheng. They're set to play their first doubles match against, ironically, Quevedo.

The final alternate is Antonia Ruzic, taking Bartunkova's place. Ruzic has only played at 125-level tournaments since the US Open, so this will be a step up in level for her.

articles.summary: Empezó el año con ranking parecido al español y lo acabará igualada a él
articles.body: Si podemos dar ya por hecho que Rafael Jódar ha sido la revelación del circuito masculino esta temporada -al margen de que hoy haya perdido la final del Masters 1.000 de Shangai, lo mismo cabe decir de la polaca polaca Maja Chwalinska, que a su vez ha ganado este domingo en la final del WTA 1000 de Wuhan (China), venciendo a la británica Sonay Kartal. Rafa Jódar era el 150 de la ATP antes del primer Grand Slam de la temporada, el Open de Australia. En aquel momento Chwalinska, de 24 años entonces, era la 145. Hoy, tras la disputa de los últimos torneos de categoría 1.000 del año, ambos estarán mañana en el puesto 11 de sus respectivos rankings profesionales. Maja jugó aún torneos WTA 125 -equivalentes a los challenger ATP- en la primera parte de la temporada, ganando en Oeiras, pero dio el salto en Roland Garros donde, partiendo de la previa, alcanzó la final. Cayó en ella ante Mirra Andreeva y luego no consiguió resultados relevantes hasta el inicio de esta gira asiática, pero el aporte de estas dos citas la ha situado al borde del 'top 10': el mismo punto que Rafa Jódar, aunque la regularidad de éste haya sido superior . En la final de Wuhan venció a la británica Sonay Kartal, que alcanzó una final de primer nivel desde el 170 WTA. En semifinales Kartal sorprendió a Jelena Ostapenko por 7-6 y 7-6, mientras que Chwalinska hizo lo propio con su compatriota y ex número 1 del mundo Iga Swiatek (7-5 y 6-1). En la final la polaca la superó por 2-6, 6-4 y 6-2 en 165 minutos de juego.

articles.title: Breaking down to build again: Andrey Rublev's bid to reinvent himself
articles.summary: Andrey Rublev has spent much of his career trying to get better at being Andrey Rublev.
articles.body: Andrey Rublev has spent much of his career trying to get better at being Andrey Rublev. Now, the mercurial Russian, whose on-court meltdowns are almost as well chronicled as his title wins, is attempting to rewrite the script that took him to world No. 5. At 28, he is trying to become a different player.Rublev has slipped to No. 23, falling outside the top 20 for the first time since January 2020 six weeks ago. For a player who finished inside the top 10 between 2020 and 2024, for five consecutive seasons, and reached 10 Grand Slam quarter-finals, the decline is striking. Yet, after 36 main-draw appearances at the majors without advancing beyond the last eight, Rublev has come to a realisation, to build something new, he must first be willing to break down what got him here.“It's not easy to change something that you know for all your life,” said Rublev, the No.4 seed at the Almaty Open, an ATP 250 event. “It’s not easy to switch that, what brought you to No.5 in the world for something else that you don't really trust yet.”The forehand, Rublev’s biggest weapon, is a useful example. It’s a shot he could turn to under pressure almost without thinking. But the instincts that once served him so well can also become constraints when he is trying to expand his game.“I’m trying to change, on and off the court, mentally, things that have become a habit, that have already taken me to the limit, with what I could do with that,” he says, eyes fixed on the table before him. “Now, it's the second part of (my) career where I try to do something different completely.”There is no guarantee the experiment will work. Rublev knows that as well as anyone.“Maybe it's going to make the second part of my career better than my first part, or maybe not,” he says, lifting his gaze and looking straight at the interviewer. “But at least I know I did something, I gave myself a chance.”“With the game I used to have, it will go down little by little until I cannot play anymore,” he says. “To be just top 30 for the next five-six years, for me, it makes no difference.”For the past 18 months, Rublev has been working with former world No. 1 Marat Safin, a partnership that pushed the 28-year-old to address mental and emotional struggles that has seen him harm himself physically on the court.Asked what has changed most since working with Safin, Rublev does not begin with tactics or results.“I'm enjoying much more the life. I'm much more in peace with myself,” he says.It is a striking answer from a player whose intensity has long been one of the defining features of his tennis.“From the past, before Marat, I was very depressed,” he says. “Taking ... antidepressant pills to don't feel depression.”He pauses, taking a deep breath, before describing how low he had felt.“Basically, it was a bit of drama that was happening to me, and I didn't know how to escape. I was at the bottom of my darkest days.”It was there, he says, that he reached a point at which he could no longer continue as he had been. He faced a choice -- to remain trapped in the same patterns or to try, finally, to do something about them.“I choose to try to fix it,” he said.Rublev is not short of reminders that reinvention is possible.“When you see players like Sasha (Zverev) or Daniil (Medvedev), when they're doing something good, it gives a clear signal that I can do it as well,” he says. “Because I know what I'm capable of. If he can do it, I can find a way as well.”Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Inspiring story of the day: “Having someone who shows up for you and believes in your fire changes everything” - How Venus Williams mid-forties romance with Andrea Preti turned into  longevity and love
articles.summary: Venus Williams has spent decades changing tennis, winning seven Grand Slam singles titles and helping secure equal prize money for women at Wimbledon.
articles.body: Venus Williams has spent decades changing tennis, winning seven Grand Slam singles titles and helping secure equal prize money for women at Wimbledon. At 46, she continues to compete despite years of physical challenges, including Sjögren’s syndrome, an autoimmune condition she publicly discussed in 2011. Away from the court, Williams has entered a new chapter with Italian actor and model Andrea Preti, whom she married in 2025. Their relationship began in 2024, and Preti has supported her return to professional tennis. Her story now brings together sporting success, personal challenges and a new marriage.How did Venus Williams rise from Compton to become a tennis legend?Venus Williams grew up in Compton, California, alongside her younger sister Serena Williams. Their father, Richard Williams, coached them from an early age, helping them prepare for a sport in which Black women were still underrepresented at the highest level.Venus turned professional in 1994, aged 14. Her powerful serve, speed and ability to compete under pressure soon made her one of the leading players in women’s tennis. She won her first Grand Slam singles title at Wimbledon in 2000, then defended it in 2001. She also won the US Open singles title in both years.Her achievements extended beyond individual trophies. Williams won five Wimbledon singles titles and two US Open singles titles. She also won four Olympic gold medals, including three in women’s doubles with Serena and one in singles at the 2000 Sydney Games.Her influence reached beyond the court. Williams played a major role in the campaign for equal prize money at the four Grand Slam tournaments. Wimbledon introduced equal prize money for men and women in 2007, making it the last of the four majors to do so. Williams won the women’s singles title that year.The achievement reflected years of work to challenge the difference in how men’s and women’s tennis was valued. Her success also helped create more opportunities for younger players who wanted to compete at the highest level.Although Serena went on to win 23 Grand Slam singles titles, Venus built her own legacy. She became a five-time Wimbledon champion, a former world No. 1 and one of the most influential figures in modern tennis. Their careers also helped bring greater attention to the Williams family’s journey from Compton to the sport’s biggest stages.How did Venus Williams manage Sjögren’s syndrome and return to tennis?Williams publicly revealed in 2011 that she had Sjögren’s syndrome after withdrawing from the US Open. The autoimmune disease can cause dry eyes and mouth, joint pain and severe fatigue. Its effects vary from person to person, and there is no known cure.For a professional tennis player, persistent fatigue can make training and competition especially difficult. Williams has spoken about how the condition affected her energy and ability to perform. She changed her approach to training and nutrition while continuing to work towards a return to her previous level.Her experience also challenged the idea that a player must leave the sport after reaching a certain age or facing a long-term health condition. Williams continued to compete on the WTA Tour, although her results and schedule changed over the years.She also pursued interests outside tennis, including fashion and business. Her clothing brand, EleVen, and her work in interior design through V Starr have given her other ways to build a career beyond professional sport.Williams’ return to competition in 2025 was another major moment. After spending more than a year away from tournaments, she played at the Mubadala Citi DC Open in Washington. She won her first singles match in nearly two years, defeating Peyton Stearns in straight sets.After that victory, she credited her fiancé with encouraging her to continue playing. Speaking during her on-court interview, Williams said: “My fiancé is here and he really encouraged me to keep playing.” The comments offered a clear glimpse into the role Preti played during her comeback.She continued competing in 2026, playing tournaments including the Australian Open, the US Open and events on the North American hard-court circuit. At the 2026 US Open, she returned to Grand Slam doubles with Serena for the first time since 2022. The sisters lost a close three-set match to Hao-Ching Chan and Maya Joint.The result did not give them another title, but their return drew attention to a partnership that has shaped tennis for more than two decades. Williams’ continued presence on the tour has also kept the focus on her determination to compete on her own terms.How did Venus Williams meet Andrea Preti and decide to marry him?Williams met Andrea Preti in 2024 at a Gucci show during Milan Fashion Week. According to Vogue, Williams had been in Lake Como on a trip with her sisters when she received an invitation to attend the event. Preti was there too, and the two began talking.Their first meeting led to further contact and dates in London. Williams told Vogue that she had spent six years single before the relationship began and wanted something straightforward. The couple became engaged on January 31, 2025, during a trip to Tuscany.Williams later spoke publicly about Preti’s support when she returned to tennis. Her comments after the DC Open victory made clear that he had encouraged her to continue competing, even as she faced the demands of professional sport.The couple first held a wedding ceremony in Ischia, Italy, on September 18, 2025. They later held a second wedding in Palm Beach, Florida, in December. The Florida celebrations included several days of events with family and friends, followed by a courthouse ceremony that made their marriage official in the United States.Explaining why they decided to hold a second wedding, Williams told Vogue: “We had this dream to do our wedding in Italy. But we didn’t have enough time to do the paperwork—because I’m a foreigner, it can take about eight months. So we decided to have a second wedding.”The celebrations included a yacht gathering arranged by Serena Williams, a family sports day and a wedding reception. Williams described the experience to Vogue as “the happiest, most beautiful, sweetest day.”The marriage marked a new chapter for Williams, who had kept much of her private life away from public attention. Their story also shows how the relationship developed alongside her return to tennis rather than after she had left the sport.What does Venus Williams’ story tell us about love, age and success?Williams’ career has never followed a simple path. She reached the top of tennis while still young, helped change the sport’s approach to equal pay and continued playing through a long-term health condition. Her achievements have come alongside years of work outside tennis and a life that has changed with time.Her relationship with Preti has added another part to that story. She has spoken openly about his encouragement during her comeback, while their wedding celebrations brought their families together in Italy and Florida.At the 2026 US Open, Williams and Serena returned to the doubles court together, reminding fans of the partnership that helped define their careers. Venus’ singles results in recent seasons have not matched her peak years, but she has continued to compete against younger players and make her own decisions about the future.Her journey is not simply about winning trophies or staying in the sport for as long as possible. It is also about making room for personal choices, new relationships and interests beyond competition.
